content: 1. The recommended intervention packages for key populations are designed to address the specific needs of young individuals within these groups. These interventions are informed by principles such as human rights, gender equality, equity, inclusion, medical ethics, universal health coverage, evidence-based public health, and community-led responses by key populations. 2. The Global AIDS Strategy 2021–2026, published by the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS, emphasizes the goal of ending inequalities and eradicating AIDS. This strategy outlines a comprehensive framework for addressing the epidemic through targeted interventions and global collaboration. 3. Differentiated antiretroviral therapy (ART) delivery models have been developed to cater to specific populations, including children, adolescents, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and other key populations. These models aim to optimize care delivery and improve health outcomes, as outlined by the World Health Organization in 2017. 4. Harm reduction strategies, such as needle exchange programs and opioid substitution therapy, have been shown to be cost-effective in reducing the transmission of HIV among people who inject drugs. This is supported by research published in the International Journal of Drug Policy in 2015. 5. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention has been demonstrated to be cost-effective among men who have sex with men in the UK, as evidenced by a modeling study and health economic evaluation published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2018. 6. A systematic review of cost-effectiveness modeling studies highlights the financial and public health impact of scaling up PrEP for HIV prevention. This review, published in PLoS Medicine in 2013, underscores the importance of expanding access to PrEP in high-risk populations. 7. Methadone maintenance therapy has been shown to be a cost-effective intervention for reducing HIV transmission among people who inject drugs. This finding is supported by research published in the American Journal of Public Health in 2000. 8. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 1948, serves as a foundational document advocating for the protection of human rights, including the right to health. 9. The International Guidelines on HIV/AIDS and Human Rights, published in 2006 by the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS, provide a framework for integrating human rights principles into HIV/AIDS policies and programs. 10. The International Code of Medical Ethics, established by the World Medical Association in 2006, outlines ethical principles for medical professionals, emphasizing the importance of patient-centered care and respect for human dignity. 11. The Lancet Commission on Global Health 2035 envisions a world converging within a generation, where health disparities are minimized, and universal health coverage is achieved. This report, published in 2013, highlights the economic and social benefits of investing in health. 12. The Greater Involvement of People Living with HIV (GIPA) principle, outlined in a policy brief by the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS in 2007, emphasizes the importance of involving individuals living with HIV in decision-making processes to enhance the effectiveness of HIV responses. 13. The World Health Organization's Handbook for Guideline Development, second edition (2014), provides a comprehensive methodology for developing evidence-based guidelines to improve health outcomes globally. 14. The Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action, adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 1993, reaffirms the commitment to human rights and the elimination of discrimination, including in the context of health. 15. The International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights (1966) and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966) establish the legal framework for the protection of fundamental human rights, including the right to health and freedom from discrimination. 16. Evidence-based guidance for eliminating HIV-related stigma and discrimination in healthcare settings has been developed to support countries in implementing effective programs. This guidance, published by the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS in 2020, focuses on six key settings. 17. Forced anal examinations to determine sexual orientation and behavior are medically unsound and constitute a violation of human rights. This practice has been condemned in a study published in PLoS Medicine in 2018. 18. A critical review of interventions to prevent sexually transmitted and bloodborne infections among sex workers in high-income countries highlights the importance of addressing structural determinants and implementing evidence-based strategies. This review was published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2019. 19. Policing practices that target people who inject drugs have been associated with increased HIV risk. A review published in Epidemiologic Reviews in 2020 emphasizes the need for harm reduction approaches and policy reform. 20. Transgender individuals face significant barriers to healthcare due to insurance denials. A study published in the Journal of General Internal Medicine in 2020 highlights the disparities in access to care based on insurance type. 21. The criminalization of drug use among people who inject drugs exacerbates HIV risks. A systematic review published in The Lancet HIV in 2017 calls for decriminalization and harm reduction strategies to mitigate these risks. 22. Legal name changes for transgender individuals may serve as a structural intervention to address social determinants of health. This potential was explored in a study published in Sex Research and Social Policy in 2018. 23. Sex work laws and associated stigma contribute to increased HIV risks among sex workers. A study published in Nature Communications in 2020 underscores the need for legal and policy reforms to protect the health and rights of sex workers. 24. Consolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections for key populations emphasize the importance of evidence-based interventions and community-led responses. These guidelines were developed by the World Health Organization. 25. A contextual review of HIV epidemics among Black men who have sex with men across the African diaspora highlights common roots and disparities. This review was published in The Lancet in 2012. 26. Associations between sex work laws and the health of sex workers were systematically reviewed in a study published in PLoS Medicine in 2018. The findings emphasize the need for decriminalization and supportive policies. 27. Reductions in access to HIV prevention and care services are linked to arrests and convictions among men who have sex with men, as reported in a global survey published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2017. 28. The global epidemiology of HIV among female sex workers is influenced by structural determinants, as highlighted in a study published in The Lancet in 2015. Addressing these determinants is critical for effective interventions. 29. Legalization of syringe access programs has been associated with reduced syringe sharing and reuse among people who inject drugs, as demonstrated in a study published in Drug and Alcohol Dependence in 2007. 30. Disparities in HIV risks among Black men who have sex with men compared to other racial groups were analyzed in a meta-analysis published in The Lancet in 2012. The findings call for targeted interventions to address these disparities. 31. Stigma in healthcare settings significantly impacts the health outcomes of people living with HIV. A study published in BMC Medicine in 2019 highlights the importance of stigma reduction programs. 32. Interventions to reduce HIV-related stigma among healthcare professionals have been shown to improve attitudes and care quality. A study published in AIDS Care in 2015 evaluated the effectiveness of a game-based experiential approach. 33. Integration of HIV care with primary healthcare services in rural Kenya has been associated with improved patient satisfaction and reduced stigma, as reported in a study published in AIDS Research and Treatment in 2013. 34. Stigma reduction training for healthcare providers in Bangladesh has improved attitudes toward marginalized populations, as demonstrated in a study published in the Journal of Adolescent Health in 2017. 35. A photovoice intervention, Recovery Speaks, was implemented to reduce stigma among primary care providers. This approach was evaluated in a study published in Psychiatric Services in 2016. 36. Brief psychoeducational programs have been effective in reducing stigma in healthcare settings, as evidenced by a study conducted in Malaysia.
